items.originalTitle: Building a real-time AI tutor for 5-year-olds
items.summary:
A team has developed an AI tutor designed to teach math and reading to children aged 4 to 9, focusing on real-time interaction with sub-second response times to keep young learners engaged. The system departs from standard AI agent loops by streaming multiple actions in a single response, allowing immediate execution of teaching steps without long pauses that can cause children to lose attention.

The developers emphasized embedding pedagogy into the AI's architecture, balancing instruction quality and latency. They created a custom harness to manage action generation and execution separately, enabling the tutor to adapt its teaching approach dynamically and validate actions without interrupting the flow. This approach aims to replicate the responsiveness and adaptability of human teachers in a digital format.

items.title: Refik Anadol's Dataland opens as world's first AI art museum with immersive rainforest exhibit using wearables and AI-trained on Amazon data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A New Experiential Gallery Just Might Change Your Mind About AI Art
items.summary:
Dataland, co-founded by artist Refik Anadol in downtown Los Angeles, launched as the world's first museum dedicated to AI art, featuring an immersive exhibit called Machine Dreams: Rainforest. The exhibit uses wearable devices to track visitors' biometrics and movements, generating dynamic digital visuals and soundscapes based on AI models trained with extensive natural science data collected from the Amazon and other rainforests.

Anadol and his team spent three years developing their own AI models using five petabytes of data sourced with researcher consent, aiming to create an ethical and environmentally responsible AI art experience. The exhibit responds interactively to visitors, incorporating scents and visual effects that simulate natural environments, challenging common perceptions of AI-generated art as simplistic or derivative.

items.summary:

The migration involved redesigning the schema to use foreign keys and running parallel instances of the old and new systems with comprehensive testing to ensure correctness.

The process included three phases: describing function intent with Claude, fixing failing tests through focused prompts, and deploying via a blue/green approach with continuous validation. Wakim emphasized that a strong test suite was crucial for trusting AI-generated code during the migration.

items.summary:

The agents operate in parallel without a central coordinator, sharing findings through version control and following a structured workflow involving reconnaissance, hunting, gap-filling, and validation. Each candidate bug must include a testable claim, a clear mechanism of failure, and a self-contained reproducer that runs against the real code to be considered a valid finding. This approach aligns with similar efforts by other organizations like Anthropic and Cloudflare, highlighting a growing methodology for AI-driven security audits.

items.originalTitle: Meta Finds a New Way to Spend a Fortune on AI
items.summary:
The AI laggards are going on the offensive! Meta Platforms on Thursday unveiled its latest AI model, Muse Spark 1.1, a day after SpaceX’s AI unit introduced a new model of its own. Like SpaceX, Meta claimed its new model delivers performance comparable to that of established models from AI labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. We’ll have to wait a few days to see whether developers agree. (Meanwhile, OpenAI unveiled its latest models, GPT 5.6).

What may be most significant, however, is Meta’s apparent intention to spend a fortune subsidizing usage of its new model in hopes of pulling market share from its rivals. In an interview with Bloomberg, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta’s pricing for what users would pay to use the models would be “very aggressive and attractive.” Bloomberg’s report said Meta’s prices would be about a quarter of those advertised by top models from Anthropic and OpenAI—in other words, dirt cheap.

It follows the two companies’ joint introduction of a new model, Grok 4.5, meant to perform engineering tasks as well as general knowledge work.

items.title: Universities Fret as Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and DeepMind Lure Their Professors [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Universities Fret as Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and DeepMind Lure Their Professors
items.summary:
Renowned university professors and academic researchers keep joining frontier AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Remaining faculty say the brain drain is threatening the development of open source AI models in the West.

So far this year, at least 22 professors and researchers have taken leave or stepped back from their roles at Stanford, Berkeley, Harvard, Virginia and the University of Southern California to work at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta Platforms, according to a review of college websites, X posts and LinkedIn profiles. The actual number of departures could be far higher, according to my conversations with professors at some of the universities.

Many of the professors are computer scientists, but some are physicists, economists, statisticians or mathematicians. Two of them taught philosophy, which probably has something to do with the philosophical questions that arise when labs shape the personalities and self-awareness of AI. (See the list below.) 

Just last week, Jelani Nelson, the chair of Berkeley’s department of electrical engineering and computer science, and UT Austin philosophy professor Harvey Lederman said they’d be taking leave to join Anthropic as members of its technical staff. (Lederman will continue teaching at New York University.)

AI professors have been leaving school for big jobs at Google and its ilk since deep learning and self-driving software got hot 15 years ago, and after the generative AI boom got rolling a couple of years ago. But Berkeley computer science professor and AI researcher Joey Gonzalez said the exits have accelerated this year.

The reason is the same as it’s always been: It’s simply more difficult to do cutting edge research in academia because it requires large amounts of expensive AI servers, which the schools generally don’t have.

Apple is on a quest to shrink powerful AI models to run on iPhones, which could cut down on cloud computing costs and enhance user privacy. But a small startup that emerged from stealth mode earlier this year says it recently got an AI model running on an iPhone bigger than any previous mobile model.

The startup, PrismML, said it has shrunk down Qwen 3.6, an open-source large language model developed by Chinese internet giant Alibaba, to run on an iPhone 17 Pro. The model has 27 billion parameters, which are roughly similar to the synapses in a brain and can help determine the complexity of the data a model can process. In contrast, most models that run on mobile phones have only a few billion parameters active at a time.
